finding: Test 5 ("Role units run concurrently and every other kind does not overlap them") has no pinned observable. The only test instrument the spec defines is `TP_RUNNER_SEAM`, whose args are fixed at `{unit_kind} {unit_id} {log_path} {max_budget_usd}` (§3.2.1) — no start/end timestamp, no run-id-scoped marker, no concurrency counter — so nothing in the recorded invocations distinguishes two overlapping children from two sequential ones. One engineer asserts wall-clock overlap (flaky), another asserts spawn order only (vacuous).
suggestion: Give the seam a recordable ordering signal (e.g. require the fake runner to append start/end timestamps or a live-sibling count to its log) and restate 5 against it: "the seam records two role invocations whose start/end intervals overlap, and no non-role invocation overlaps any other".

finding: Test 20 asserts "A `runner.env` entry for `TP_UNATTENDED` does not reach the child". §5.1 says `tp run` sets `TP_UNATTENDED=1` for every child, and §3.2 says the driver's variables are applied after the `env` merge, so the variable does reach the child — it is the entry's *value* that is discarded. One engineer asserts the variable is absent from the child's environment (which would fail), another asserts it equals `1`.
suggestion: Reword 20: "A `runner.env` entry setting `TP_UNATTENDED=0` does not take effect: the child's `TP_UNATTENDED` is `1` and the unattended refusals still fire."

finding: Test 21's last clause — "An exit 2 with no escalation record is a unit failure instead" — conflates a failed *attempt* with `stop_reason: unit-failure`. §5.2 says such a unit "is judged by its §3.3 predicate and its exit code as usual", and §3.4 sets `unit-failure` only when a unit "exhausted its attempts" — with the default `run_max_unit_retries` of 1 a single exit 2 is retried, not a stop. The assertion's expected `stop_reason` depends on an unstated retry setting.
suggestion: Pin the retry count in the test: "…with `run_max_unit_retries` 0, an exit 2 with no escalation record is a failed attempt that stops the run with `unit-failure`; with retries left it is retried instead."

finding: Test 32 requires `--merge` to "exit 1 when an input has lines and none parsed". §8a.4 conditions exit 1 on "at least one content line, none of which parsed" and explicitly excludes blank/whitespace-only lines; test 49 requires exit 0 on "a file of only blank lines" — a file that has lines and parses none. Two engineers write contradictory tests from 32 and 49.
suggestion: Change 32 to "exits 1 when an input has at least one content line and none of them parsed" and add "whitespace-only lines are not content lines", matching §8a.4 and test 49.

finding: Test 45 asserts `next_units` "omits every role whose findings file is already present", but §4.1 omits only a role whose file "already satisfies §3.3's predicate — present and wholly parseable". Test 48 and test 52 assert the opposite of test 45 for the present-but-malformed case (the role must be re-run, not skipped), so the three tests cannot all pass as written.
suggestion: Reword 45 to "omits every role whose findings file satisfies §3.3's predicate (present and wholly parseable), and returns a role whose file is present but holds an unparseable line", so 45, 48 and 52 pin one condition.

finding: Round 9 propagated the role predicate "present and wholly parseable" to §4.1, §6.2 and §3.3, but §3.1 still carries the old present-only form: "The oracle decides the unit set first, omitting roles whose file is already present (§4.1)", and its justification sentence "A leftover therefore either means the role is done and is not re-run, or the role is being re-run and its leftover is gone before it starts" is false under the new predicate — a leftover that is malformed means the role is NOT done and IS re-run. §3.1 is the section the driver implementer reads, so the one component round 9 did not update is the one that skips a malformed file.
suggestion: Change §3.1 to "omitting roles whose findings file already satisfies §3.3's predicate — present and wholly parseable (§4.1)", and rewrite the leftover sentence to name the three cases: satisfied predicate (not re-run), failed predicate (re-run, file deleted first), absent (run).

finding: Round 9's `audit-fix` row pins the durable write as "That row carries a disposition in the round's results file" and names `tp audit --resolve <results.ndjson>` as the mechanism, but no section defines where that results file lives. Role files are `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` and `audit-record`'s durable write is "an audit round file", while `--resolve` operates on the merged NDJSON the record unit produced at an agent-chosen path (§6.3 only says the record unit merges `$TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson`). The same hole sits in `review-resolve`'s "the round's file". This breaks §3.3's own load-bearing claim that every predicate is "decidable by reading one file": the driver cannot decide a predicate over a file whose path it was never told.
suggestion: Name the merged results path deterministically — e.g. `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson`, written by the record unit — and use it in both the `audit-fix` and `review-resolve` predicate cells and in the `--resolve` invocation.

finding: The eight `stop_reason` rows define why a run stops but never define what `tp run` exits with. Only three exit codes appear anywhere in the spec: 0 for `converged` (§3.1 step 2), 4 for the run-lock conflict (§3.1), and 2 for usage errors (§3.2.1). `escalation`, `unit-failure`, `no-units`, `interrupted`, `cap-units`, `cap-wall-clock` and `cap-budget` have no exit code at all, so the implementer must invent seven of them — and the operator wrapping `tp run` in cron/CI has nothing to branch on, which is the exact distinction §8a.5 spends a section preserving for every other command.
suggestion: Add an `Exit` column to §3.4's table fixing the code for each stop_reason (e.g. 0 converged; 3 escalation as a normal expected outcome needing a human; 1 unit-failure/no-units; 1 or a distinct code for each cap; interrupted), and add a §10.1 test asserting the code per reason.

finding: The fence accepts any cap value equal to or below the resolved one, justified by "lowering a budget cannot manufacture convergence". But §3.4 and §7 give 0 an inverted meaning for both budget fields: run_max_budget_usd 0 is "disabled" and run_max_unit_budget_usd 0 means the runner's own budget flag is omitted entirely. So an unattended unit may run `tp set --workflow run_max_budget_usd=0`, exit 0 under the fence, and remove the very cap that bounds unbounded spend — exactly the hatch §5.1 says it closes for run_max_units and run_max_wall_clock_seconds.
suggestion: State that for fields where 0 is a disable sentinel, the fence compares effective strictness rather than numeric magnitude: under TP_UNATTENDED, setting run_max_budget_usd or run_max_unit_budget_usd to 0 when the resolved value is non-zero exits 2 like a raise. Add a test row to §10.3 item 19 for the 0 case.

finding: Test 52 requires the oracle, the driver and the Stop hook to "apply the same role predicate", and §6.2 says the hook "applies §3.3's predicate ... the same condition the driver and the oracle use". But the hook is a plugin-shipped shell script with a 10s timeout (§6.4) and no tp subcommand is specified that evaluates the predicate, so the only buildable route is a third, hand-written NDJSON parser inside the hook. That parser will disagree with Go's `encoding/json` on the edges the spec itself cares about (trailing-comma lines from §8a.4, whitespace-only lines, a truncated final line with no newline), and the disagreement is invisible until an unattended round silently skips or re-runs a role.
suggestion: Specify one tp entry point that decides the predicate — e.g. `tp run --check-unit` (or `tp review --check-file <path>`) exiting 0/1 — and require the hook, the driver and the oracle to call it, so §3.3 has exactly one implementation. Name it in §3.3, §4.1 and §6.2, and make test 52 assert all three go through it.

finding: Test 16 requires every §7 field to "accept both range endpoints and reject one step outside each", but two of §7's seven rows have no endpoints (`runner`: "Built-in name or object"; `notify_cmd`: "Any command string"), and for the decimal-dollar fields (`run_max_budget_usd` 0-10000, `run_max_unit_budget_usd` 0-1000) "one step" is undefined — 10001, 10000.01 and 10000.001 are all defensible, as are -1 and -0.01 at the low end.
suggestion: Split 16: numeric fields get the endpoint/one-step assertion with the step pinned (state whether budgets are validated as decimals and what the rejection boundary is, e.g. "any value > the maximum or < the minimum"); `runner` and `notify_cmd` get their own validity assertions (unknown built-in name rejected, map missing `default` rejected).

finding: Test 18's first clause — "Each durable-write predicate is decidable from one file with no baseline" — is a property of the design, not an observable outcome; no pass/fail assertion can be written against it (any implementation passes by inspection). Only the second clause (`audit-fix` with no code change passes) is testable.
suggestion: Replace the first clause with per-kind assertions that would fail under a delta-based predicate, e.g. "a `decompose` unit whose task file already held tasks before the unit ran still passes" and "a `review-resolve` unit passes when every finding already carried a disposition at unit start".

finding: §3.2's runner has three shapes — built-in name, object, and a per-kind map with a required `default` key whose absence is a usage error — plus a second built-in template (`opencode`, no budget flag, no `spend_key`) and the rule that every child is spawned with stdin closed (§3.2.1). §10 tests none of these: test 10 covers placeholder resolution only, and §3.2.2's per-kind accrual and run-start naming of unmetered kinds is likewise unasserted. The stdin rule is a named §2 lesson with no test.
suggestion: Add tests: a per-kind map routes each kind to its runner and a map without `default` exits 2 before any spawn; the `opencode` template passes no budget flag and reports `spend` null; under a per-kind map the run-start report names the unmetered kinds and `cap-budget` accrues only the reporting ones; a child's stdin is closed (a runner reading stdin sees EOF rather than blocking).

finding: §4.2 pins `last_failure`'s object shape `{unit_kind, unit_id, phase, exit_code, summary, at}`, requires `summary` to be tp-authored (the failing command, and the gate's own output when a gate failed) and "never the child's prose", and names a second trigger — a close with a failed quality gate. Test 23 asserts only the non-zero-exit trigger, the path, the surfacing and the clearing rule; the field set, the authorship guarantee (the concrete instance of Non-Goal 6) and the gate trigger are untested.
suggestion: Extend 23 or add a test: a close whose quality gate fails writes `last_failure` with `exit_code` from the gate and `summary` containing the gate command and its output, and a child whose stdout contains a plausible failure narrative contributes no bytes to `summary`.

finding: §6.2 deliberately scopes the Stop hook to kinds whose `TP_UNIT_KIND` ends in `-role`, and states the driver — not the hook — checks the other six kinds. Tests 26 and 39 exercise only role units, so nothing asserts the negative: an `implement` or `review-record` unit that ends without its durable write must not be blocked by the hook. That negative is the guard against the "agent that can never finish" §6.2 warns about.
suggestion: Add: "the Stop hook does not fire for a unit whose `TP_UNIT_KIND` does not end in `-role`, even when that unit's durable write is absent; the driver still records the attempt as failed."

finding: Test 31 requires exit 2 "for every command, including cobra's own built-ins". §8a.5 scopes the change to "Every command's `Args` validator" and says nothing about cobra-generated commands (`help`, `completion`), whose argument handling tp does not author. The test asserts a behaviour the section never requires, so it is unfalsifiable against the spec.
suggestion: Either drop "including cobra's own built-ins" from 31, or add the requirement to §8a.5 explicitly (naming which generated commands are wrapped) so the test has a normative source.

finding: Test 37 asserts `TP_ROUND_DIR` is "derived from phase and round", and §3.1 fixes the path as `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND` — so the exact `phase` strings are load-bearing for a path assertion. The spec names only one phase value (`release`, §4.1); tests 2 and 14 additionally use "implement", "review", "audit" as prose. Two engineers write different expected directories (`review-r3` vs `review-loop-r3`) with no way to tell which is right.
suggestion: Enumerate the `phase` values `tp resume` can report in §4.1 (with the exact strings used in `TP_ROUND_DIR`), and have tests 2, 14 and 37 cite that list.

finding: Test 45 pins the stale predicate — "A resumed round's `next_units` omits every role whose findings file is already present" — which a malformed-file role satisfies. It therefore passes against exactly the behaviour test 52 ("the oracle, the driver and the Stop hook apply the same role predicate: a role that left a malformed file is re-run, not skipped") forbids, so the two tests in the same section can both pass only by accident of fixture choice.
suggestion: Reword test 45 to "omits every role whose findings file already satisfies §3.3's predicate, and does not omit a role whose file exists but holds an unparseable line".

finding: The new §10.7 says "`tp resume`'s JSON shape gains `next_units` and `last_failure`", but §4.1 adds a third key in the same breath — `round`, "alongside" `next_units`, and explicitly not one of the existing fields ("`round` and the existing `phase`"). Test 38 asserts `round` is carried. The invalidation inventory that round 9 split out therefore under-reports the shape change it exists to catalogue, and assertions pinning `tp resume`'s exact object set will fail outside the task the inventory assigns them to.
suggestion: List all three: "`tp resume`'s JSON shape gains `next_units`, `round` and `last_failure`".

finding: `TP_RUN_DIR` is pinned as "the absolute path of `.tp/runs/$TP_RUN_ID`" while `TP_ROUND_DIR` is given only as `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND` — a repo-relative string. Test 37 pins `TP_RUN_DIR` absolute and asks only that `TP_ROUND_DIR` be "derived from phase and round". The form is load-bearing in two places: §6.3's agent definitions allow writing exactly `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, and permission matchers on a relative path behave differently from an absolute one; and the Stop hook (§6.2) resolves the same string against whatever cwd the harness left it in.
suggestion: State that `TP_ROUND_DIR` is absolute, like `TP_RUN_DIR`, and extend test 37 to assert absoluteness for both.

finding: The `runner` field may be "a map from unit kind to either of those with a `default` key covering the rest", and the only stated error is "A map missing `default` is a usage error". Nothing says what happens to a key that is not one of §3.3's eight kinds — a typo like `"audit_role"` or `"audit-roles"` silently falls through to `default` and the operator's whole point in configuring the map (running audits on a different model, §3.2) is silently lost. `tp validate --project` (§7) must decide this, and the implementer has to invent the answer.
suggestion: State that a map key other than the eight kinds in §3.3's table or `default` is a usage error (exit 2) raised at resolution time, reported by `tp validate --project` and `tp config --resolved`, and add it to test 16 or 10.

finding: Spend reading has exactly one defined failure: a runner that declares no `spend_key` reports `spend: null`. Three runtime failures of a *declared* key have no behaviour: the final log line is not JSON at all (a crashed harness, a plain-text error), the dot path is absent from an otherwise valid line, and the value is present but non-numeric. Each needs a decision an implementer cannot derive — is it `spend: null` for that unit, a failed attempt, or a run-level stop — and it directly changes whether `cap-budget` is trustworthy, since a silently-null unit makes the accrued total an undercount of the same kind §3.2.2's per-kind clause exists to prevent.
suggestion: State the rule: a declared `spend_key` that cannot be read from the final line records `spend: null` for that unit, never fails the unit, and marks the run's spend total as partial in `--status` (the same wording as the unmetered-kinds report). Add it to test 11.

finding: The audit-fix kind cannot address its own artifact from the contract as written. Its durable write is "that row carries a disposition in the round's results file", and it disposes with `tp audit --resolve <results.ndjson> <idx> …` using a 0-based index — but no section defines where the merged audit results file lives (§6.3 only says record units merge `$TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson`, not where the merged output is written), and §3.1 gives the unit id as `role:item_id`, which is not an index. Neither the unit nor the driver's predicate can resolve a path or an index from what the oracle supplies.
suggestion: Name the merged results path explicitly (e.g. `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson`, written by the audit-record unit) and state how `role:item_id` maps to the 0-based index — either the oracle carries the index in the unit entry, or `tp audit --resolve` accepts `role:item_id` in place of an index. Extend §10.6 item 53 to assert the mapping.

finding: `audit-fix`'s unit id is `role:item_id` (§3.1) but its command is `tp audit --resolve <results.ndjson> <idx> ...` — a 0-based index into a file. Neither the mapping from `role:item_id` to `<idx>`, nor the path of "the round's results file", is given anywhere: §6.3 names only the per-role inputs (`$TP_ROUND_DIR/*.ndjson`) that the record unit merges, not where the merged/recorded results land. So the unit cannot construct its command and the driver cannot open a file to evaluate the kind's durable-write predicate after the child exits (§6.2 requires it to, for all eight kinds).
suggestion: Name the round's results file path explicitly (e.g. `$TP_ROUND_DIR/merged.ndjson`, written by `audit-record`) and state how `role:item_id` resolves to the index — either the brief carries the resolved index, or `tp audit --resolve` accepts `role:item_id` in place of `<idx>`. Extend test 53 to cover the id-to-row lookup.

finding: §3.1 fixes an `audit-fix` unit's `id` as the finding's `role:item_id`, but round 9's disposition mechanism is `tp audit --resolve <results.ndjson> <idx> …` keyed by 0-based index. Nothing maps one to the other, so neither the unit (which receives `TP_UNIT_ID`) nor the driver (which must test "that row carries a disposition") can locate the row without re-deriving the index by scanning, and any rewrite of the file that reorders rows silently redirects the disposition to a different finding.
suggestion: State that `--resolve`'s index is positional in the file the record unit froze and that the file's row order is stable, and specify how a unit resolves its `role:item_id` to that index — or give `tp audit --resolve` a `role:item_id` form so the unit id is the key it is addressed by.

finding: The stop-reason precedence is justified by evaluation order — "`converged` leads because §3.1 checks releasability before caps" — but the rest of the list contradicts that justification: `no-units` is decided at §3.1 step 3 and every cap at step 6, yet `no-units` is ranked last, below all three caps. The stated principle and the stated order cannot both be right, which leaves §10.5 item 34 ("two simultaneously satisfied stop conditions record the higher-precedence reason") without a derivable expectation for the no-units-plus-cap pair.
suggestion: Drop the evaluation-order rationale and justify the order on reporting value alone (an escalation or unit failure tells the operator more than an exhausted cap), or move `no-units` above the cap rows so the order matches §3.1's sequence. Then name the concrete pair item 34 asserts.

finding: `cap-units` counts "Spawned children", caps are "evaluated between iterations only", and the stated overshoot allowance covers only wall-clock and budget ("a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration"). An iteration of N concurrent role units can push the spawned count past `run_max_units` mid-iteration, and the spec never says whether the driver spawns the whole iteration, spawns only the remaining allowance (which would leave a round with missing role files and a record unit merging an incomplete set), or refuses the iteration. All three are buildable and they produce different artifacts.
suggestion: State that unit iterations are spawned whole and `run_max_units` is checked only between iterations — extending the existing overshoot sentence to name units alongside wall-clock and budget — so a round never runs a partial role set. Assert it in test 3 or 5.

finding: Two path templates embed the unit id verbatim — `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` here and `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` in §3.3/§6.3 — while §3.1 defines ids that are not path-safe tokens: `role:item_id` for audit-fix (a colon) and "the spec base name" for review-resolve and decompose (which can carry dots and, if a spec sits in a subdirectory, separators). No section states a sanitization or rejection rule, so the log path, the §6.3 write allowlist and the Stop hook's predicate path are each derived from an unvalidated string.
suggestion: State the id-to-path rule once in §3.1: ids are constrained to `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` or are slugified before substitution into any path, and the spec base name means the basename without directories. Add an assertion to §10.5 item 37 that an audit-fix unit's log path and a subdirectory spec's ids produce single path segments.

finding: Round 9 pinned unit success as exit 0 AND durable write present (§3.3, test 51), but §4.2 still triggers `last_failure` only "when a unit exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate", and test 23 repeats "on a non-zero unit exit". The newly named failure mode — exit 0 with the durable write absent — therefore records nothing, so the next attempt re-enters the same wall with no idea the previous one hit it, which is precisely the continuity gap §4.2 exists to close.
suggestion: Restate §4.2's trigger as "when a unit fails its §3.3 success test (non-zero exit, or exit 0 with the durable write absent), or closes with a failed quality gate", with a tp-authored `summary` naming the missing durable write; update test 23 to match.

finding: §5.1's table names four exact commands whose refusal is buildable and testable. The prose then adds "`runner` and `notify_cmd` are fenced too, and more strictly: ... under the variable a unit cannot set them at all, at any layer", and test 40 restates it — but no command surface is named. `runner` is a workflow field, so the candidate surfaces are at least `tp set --workflow runner=`, a `tp run --runner`-style CLI flag if one exists, and whatever writes `.tp/local.json` for `notify_cmd`; the implementer must guess which of these refuse, with which exit code and which hint, and a missed surface is a hole in the one fence that governs commands the *driver* executes.
suggestion: Add two rows to §5.1's table in the same form as the other four — `tp set --workflow runner=` and whatever command writes `notify_cmd` into `.tp/local.json` — each with "Exit 2, same shape", and state that reading the field from the env layer is ignored under the variable (already covered by the paragraph below).

finding: §4.1 adds `next_units` (an ordered array of `{kind, id, brief_command}`) to `tp resume` as the *driver's* machine surface, while §6.2 makes the SessionStart hook inject `tp resume --compact` into every child unit. The spec never says whether `next_units` survives `--compact`, so on the plain reading every unit's context is seeded with the brief commands of units it must not run — bytes that feed no decision the unit makes (its own work arrives via `{prompt}` + `brief_command`, §3.2.1), and an active misdirection risk since a unit handed a list of pending briefs may run more than its one unit. §7 pins `--compact` behaviour only for run state (`stop_reason` and cap totals survive; per-unit rows stripped), leaving the resume payload the hook actually ships unspecified.
suggestion: State in §4.1 (and mirror in §6.2) that `next_units` and `round` are emitted under `--json` only and are stripped by `--compact`, so the hook payload carries orientation plus `last_failure` and nothing about units the child will not execute; add a test to §10.4 asserting the SessionStart payload contains no `next_units`.

finding: §7 opens "New project-level defaults, resolving at read time through the existing layered path" and then exempts `notify_cmd` as per-operator, read from `.tp/local.json` only — yet the next paragraph says `tp config --resolved`, `tp config --extract` and `tp validate --project` cover ALL the new fields "on the same terms as every existing workflow field". `--extract` writes project config and `--project` validates project config, so both would handle a field that by definition can never appear there; §10.2 item 16 asserts the local-only rule but nothing pins the tooling exception.
suggestion: Scope the tooling sentence: `--resolved` covers all seven fields; `--extract` and `--project` cover the six project-level ones and reject or ignore `notify_cmd`. Reword §7's opening so it does not classify `notify_cmd` as a project-level default.

finding: §8a.4 and §3.3 apply two different validity thresholds to the same role file. §3.3's predicate fails on ANY unparseable line, and §4.1/§10.6 item 52 make the oracle, driver and Stop hook all enforce it; --merge instead skips bad lines and only exits 1 when NO content line parsed. Inside a run the strict predicate fires first, so the merge's exit-1 case is unreachable (the role unit is a failed attempt and the run stops with unit-failure long before review-record runs), while the case that IS reachable in a run — a file with some parseable and some malformed lines — is precisely what --merge silently undercounts. §8a.4's stated motivation ("an unattended driver reads the exit code alone") therefore does not describe how the two components actually interact.
suggestion: Either align the thresholds (make --merge exit 1 whenever any input has a skipped content line, matching §3.3) or state explicitly that §8a.4 protects the operator-driven merge path outside `tp run`, and note in §8a.4 that inside a run the §3.3 predicate is the earlier and stricter guard.

finding: §8a.5 says every Args validator exits 2, "matching §9's definition of a usage error". §9 is Non-Goals and contains no definition of a usage error or any exit-code table; no section of this spec defines one. The claim the arity change is anchored to is a dangling reference, so the rule's authority is unstated (elsewhere the spec cites §9 correctly by item, e.g. "Non-Goal 6" in §3.2.2).
suggestion: Point the reference at the real authority — tp's documented exit-code table in skills/tp/REFERENCE.md (0 success, 1 validation, 2 usage, 3 file, 4 state) — or state the definition inline in §8a.5 and drop the §9 citation.

finding: Test 12 calls the run state "a run.json row"; §3.5 and test 15 name the file `.tp/run-<base>.json`. The bare `run.json` reads as a fixed filename and would send an implementer to the wrong path.
suggestion: Change 12 to "A `.tp/run-<base>.json` row exists with null `exit_code` before its child exits and is updated after".

finding: Test 24's "its hook payloads are asserted against fixtures" does not pin what a fixture contains. The `SessionStart` payload is `tp resume --compact` (§6.2), whose content varies with cycle state, so a literal fixture comparison is either brittle or vacuous, and the test does not say which hooks have fixtures.
suggestion: Restate as a structural assertion: "the `SessionStart` hook emits exactly the bytes of `tp resume --compact` for the same cycle state (compared against a freshly computed value, not a frozen string), and the `PreToolUse`/`Stop` hooks emit the documented decision objects."

finding: Round 9 split the test list at 40/41, leaving §10.5 titled "Signals the driver reads" — the title of §8a — while only tests 28-32 map to §8a's five defects. Tests 33-40 cover attempt counting (§3.4), stop-reason precedence (§3.4), `run_state` (§3.5), round-directory survival (§3.1), child environment (§3.1), `next_units` shape (§4.1), the Stop hook (§6.2) and the unattended env fence (§5.1). A test inventory whose section headings no longer name the spec sections the tests derive from is the exact drift a mechanized inventory check reads as coverage.
suggestion: Move tests 33-40 into §10.6 ("Invariants across components") or into the §10.1-10.4 sections that own their subjects, leaving §10.5 as the 28-32 block that mirrors §8a.1-8a.5.

finding: The `### 10.6 Invariants across components` heading added in round 9 is written directly on the line after test 40's continuation line, with no blank line separating it from the preceding list item.
suggestion: Insert a blank line before the `### 10.6` heading, matching every other heading in the file.

finding: §10.7 names only `next_units` and `last_failure` as the additions to `tp resume`'s JSON shape, but §4.1 also adds a top-level `round` key, and §10.7's own rule is that "every assertion pinning its exact object set moves in the same task as the field". A test pinning resume's key set would fail on `round` without any task owning the change.
suggestion: Add `round` to §10.7's first sentence alongside `next_units` and `last_failure`.

finding: `last_failure` is a single per-base file written by two different writers (the driver on a non-zero exit, `tp done` on a failed gate) and §3.3 permits concurrent role siblings, so two failing siblings in one iteration write the same path in the same instant. §3.5 specifies temp+rename for the run state precisely because "concurrent siblings write rows in the same iteration", yet §4.2 states no atomicity or locking rule — only that a second failure overwrites the first.
suggestion: Apply §3.5's rule to §4.2: the write is atomic (temp + rename), last writer wins, and the clear-on-success comparison reads the file it is about to replace. Add the concurrent-siblings case to §10.3 item 23.

finding: §6.3 says the reviewer and auditor agents "may write exactly one path — their own findings file — and are denied every other write", but §5.2 makes escalation a normal outcome for any unit, and §6.2's Stop hook explicitly excuses a role unit that produced `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json`. §10.4 item 26 asserts that escape hatch for role units specifically. Whether `tp escalate` counts as one of the denied writes is left to the reader.
suggestion: State in §6.3 that the restriction covers file-writing tools only, and that the escalation record — written by tp, not by the agent's Write tool — is unaffected; or list `$TP_RUN_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-escalation.json` as a second permitted path.

finding: `notify_cmd` "is read from `.tp/local.json` only", and test 16 asserts that, but neither says where inside that file it lives. `.tp/local.json` today holds the `active` pointer plus CLI-flag `defaults`, so an implementer must choose between a top-level `notify_cmd` key and a key under `defaults`, and the choice is what `tp config --resolved` and any future writer have to agree on.
suggestion: Name the exact JSON path (e.g. top-level `"notify_cmd"`), and pin it in test 16.
